source_text: Sed omittamus sane testimonia prophetarum, ne minus idonea probatio uideatur esse de his quibus omnino non creditur. ueniamus ad auctores et eos ipsos ad ueri probationem testes citemus, quibus contra nos uti solent, poetas dico ac philosophos. ex his unum deum probemus necesse est, non quod illi habuerint cognitam ueritatem, sed quod ueritatis ipsius tanta uis est, ut nemo possit esse tam caecus, quin uideat ingerentem se oculis diuinam claritatem. poetae igitur quamuis deos carminibus ornauerint et eorum res gestas amplificauerint summis laudibus, saepissime tamen confitentur spiritu uel mente una contineri regique omnia. Orpheus, qui est uetustissimus poetarum et aequalis ipsorum deorum, siquidem traditur inter Argonautas cum Tyndaridis et Hercule nauigasse, deum uerum et magnum πρωτόγονον appellat, quod ante ipsum nihil sit genitum, sed ab ipso sint cuncta generata. eundem etiam Φάνητα nominat, quod cum adhuc nihil esset, primus ex infinito apparuerit et extiterit. cuius onginem atque naturam quia concipere animo non poterat, ex aere inmenso natum esse dixit: πρωτόγονος Φαέθων περιμήϰεος ἠέρος υἱός. aliut enim amplius quod diceret non habebat. hunc ait esse omnium deorum parentem, quorum causa caelum condiderit liberisque prospexerit, ut haberent habitaculum sedemque communem: ἔϰτισεν ἀθανάτοις δόμον άϕθιτον. natura igitur et ratione ducente intellexit esse praestantissimam potestatem, caeli ac terrae conditricem. non poterat enim dicere Iouem esse principem rerum, qui erat Saturno genitus, neque ipsum Saturnum, qui caelo natus ferebatur; caelum autem tamquam deum primum constituere non audebat, quod uidebat elementum esse mundi, quod ipsum eguerit auctore. haec eum ratio perduxit ad deum illum primogenitum, cui adsignat et tribuit principatum. Homerus nihil nobis dare potuit quod pertineat ad ueritatem: qui humana potius quam diuina conscripsit. potuit Hesiodus, qui deorum generationem unius libri opere conplexus est: sed tamen nihil dedit non a deo conditore sumens exordium, sed a chao, quod est rudis inordinataeque materiae confusa congeries, cum explanare ante debuerit chaos ipsum unde quando quomodo esse aut constare coepisset. nimirum sicut ab aliquo artifice disposita ordinata effecta sunt omnia, sic ipsam materiam fictam esse ab aliquo necesse est. quis igitur hanc nisi deus fecit, cuius potestati subiacent omnia? sed refugit hoc ille, dum horret incognitam ueritatem. non enim Musarum instinctu sicut uideri uolebat in Helicone carmen illut effudit, sed meditatus uenerat ac paratus. nostrorum primus Maro non longe afuit a ueritate, cuius de summo deo, quem mentem ac spiritum nominauit, haec uerba sunt: principio caelum ac terras camposque liquentis lucentemque globum lunae Titaniaque astra spiritus intus alit totamque infusa per artus mens agitat molem et magno se corpore miscet. ac ne quis forte ignoraret, quisnam esset ille spiritus qui tantum haberet potestatis, declarauit alio loco dicens: deum namque ire per omnis terrasque tractusque maris caelumque profundum; hinc pecudes armenta uiros genus omne ferarum, quemque sibi tenuis nascentem accersere uitas. Ouidius quoque in principio praeclari operis sine ulla nominis dissimulatione a deo, quem fabricatorem mundi, quem rerum opificem uocat, mundum fatetur instructum. quodsi uel Orpheus uel hi nostri quae natura ducente senserunt in perpetuum defendissent, eandem quam nos sequimur doctrinam conprehensa ueritate tenuissent. Sed hactenus de poetis. ad philosophos ueniamus, quorum grauior est auctoritas certiusque iudicium, quia noti rebus commenticiis, sed inuestigandae ueritati studuisse creduntur. Thales Milesius, qui unus e septem sapientium numero fuit quique primus omnium quaesisse de causis naturalibus traditur, aquam esse dixit ex qua nata sint omnia, deum autem esse mentem quae ex aqua cuncta formauerit. ita materiam rerum posuit in umore, principium causamque nascendi constituit in deo. Pythagoras ita definiuit quid esset deus: animus per uniuersas mundi partes omnemque naturam commeans atque diffusus, ex quo omnia quae nascuntur animalia uitam capiunt. Anaxagoras deum esse dicit infinitam mentem quae per se ipsam moueatur: Antisthenes multos quidem esse populares deos, unum tamen naturalem id est summae totius artificem. Cleanthes et Anaximenes aethera esse dicunt summum deum, cui opinioni poeta noster adsensit: tum pater omnipotens fecundis imbribus aether coniugis in gremium laetae descendit et omnis magnus alit magno permixtus corpore fetus. Chrysippus naturalem uim diuina ratione praeditam, interdum diuinam necessitatem deum nuncupat, item Zenon naturalem diuinamque legem. horum omnium sententia quamuis sit incerta, eodem tamen spectat, ut prouidentiam unam esse consentiant. siue enim natura siue aether siue ratio siue mens siue fatalis necessitas siue diuina lex siue quid aliut dixeris, idem est quod a nobis dicitur deus. nec obstat appellationum diuersitas, cum ipsa significatione ad unum omnia reuoluantur. Anstoteles quamuis secum lpse dissideat ac repugnantia sibi et dicat et sentiat, in summum tamen unam mentem mundo praeesse testatur. Plato, qui omnium sapientissimus iudicatur, monarchian plane aperteque defendit nec aethera aut rationem aut naturam, sed ut est deum nominat: ah eo mundum hunc perfectum atque mirabilem esse fabricatum. quem Cicero secutus atque imitatus in plurimis frequenter deum confitetur ac supremum uocat in iis libris quos de legibus scripsit; ab eoque regi mundum argumentatur, cum disputat de natura deorum, hoc modo: nihil est praestantius deo. ab eo igitur mundum regi necesse est. nulli igitur est naturae oboediens aut subiectus deus. omnem ergo regit ipse naturam. quia autem sit deus, m uonsoiatione dehmt: nec uero deus ipse, qui intellegitur a nobis, alio modo intellegi potest nisi mens soluta quaedam et libera, segregata ab omni concretione mortali, omnia sentiens I et mouens. Annaeus quoque Seneca, qui ex Romanis uel acerrimus Stoicus fuit, quam saepe summum deum merita. laude prosequitur! nam cum de inmatura morte dissereret, non intellegis inquit auctoritatem ac maiestatem iudicis tui, rectoris orbis terrarum caelique et deorum omnium dei, a quo ista numina quae singula adoramus et colimus suspensa sunt? item in Exhortationibus: hic cum prima fundamenta molis pulcherrimae iaceret et hoc ordiretur quo neque maius quicquam nouit natura nec melius, ut omnia sub ducibus suis irent, quamuis ipse per totum se corpus intenderat, tamen ministros regni sui deus genuit. et quam multa alia de deo nostris similia locutus est! quae nunc differo, quod aliis locis opportuniora sunt. nunc satis est demonstrare summo ingenio uiros attigisse ueritatem ac paene tenuisse, nisi eos retrorsus infucata prauis opinionibus consuetudo rapuisset, qua et deos esse alios opinabantur et ea quae in usum hominis deus fecit, tamquam sensu praedita essent, pro diis habenda et colenda credebant.
thought_title: Proof of One God from Non-Christian Authors
pass_a_gloss: But let us omit the testimonies of the prophets, lest the proof seem less suitable for those who do not believe in them at all. Let us come to the authors and cite them as witnesses to the proof of the truth, those whom they are accustomed to use against us, I mean the poets and philosophers. From these, we must prove one God, not because they had known the truth, but because the power of truth itself is so great that no one can be so blind as not to see the divine clarity being forced upon their eyes. Therefore, the poets, although they have adorned the gods with their songs and amplified their deeds with the highest praises, nevertheless very often confess that all things are contained and ruled by one spirit or mind. Orpheus, who is the most ancient of the poets and a contemporary of the gods themselves, since he is said to have sailed among the Argonauts with Tyndaridis and Hercules, calls the true and great God 'protogonos', because nothing was generated before him, but all things were generated from him. He also names him 'Phaneta', because when nothing else existed, he first appeared and existed out of the infinite. Because he could not conceive of his origin and nature in his mind, he said that he was born from the immense air: 'Protogonos Phaethon, son of vast air'. For he had nothing else to say. He says that this God is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he created the heaven and provided for his children, so that they might have a common dwelling and seat: 'He created a house for the immortals that does not perish'. Therefore, led by nature and reason, he understood that there is a most excellent power, the creator of heaven and earth. For he could not say that Jupiter was the principle of things, who was born from Saturn, nor could he say that Saturn was, who was said to be born from heaven; but he did not dare to establish heaven as the first god, because he saw that it was an element of the world, which itself needed an author. This reasoning led him to that primary God, to whom he assigns and attributes the principle. Homer could not give us anything that pertains to the truth, for he wrote about human rather than divine things. Hesiod could have, who encompassed the generation of the gods in one book, but nevertheless, he did not give anything that did not take its beginning from the chaos, which is a confused mass of raw and disordered matter, when he ought to have explained beforehand what chaos is, whence, when, and how it began to exist. For just as all things were disposed, ordered, and made by some craftsman, so it is necessary that this matter itself was made by someone. Who, therefore, made it, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shuns this, fearing the unknown truth. For he did not pour out that song on Helicon by the instinct of the Muses, as he wished to appear, but came meditated and prepared. Our first poet, Maro, was not far from the truth, who said about the highest God, whom he named mind and spirit, these words: 'In the beginning, the spirit nourishes the heaven and the earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titania stars, and the mind, infused throughout, agitates the whole mass and mixes with the great body'. And lest anyone might be ignorant of who this spirit is, who has so much power, he declared in another place, saying: 'For God goes through all the lands and the tracts of the sea and the deep heaven; from him, the flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, and every living thing that is born, is summoned to life'. Ovid also, at the beginning of his renowned work, without any dissimulation of the name, confesses that the world was instructed by God, whom he calls the maker of the world and the craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our poets, led by nature, had defended what they perceived in perpetuity, they would have held the same doctrine, having grasped the truth. But so much for the poets. Let us come to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment more certain, because they are believed to have studied not fictional things, but to investigate the truth. Thales of Miletus, who was one of the seven sages and is said to have been the first to seek the natural causes, said that water is the source from which all things were born, but God is the mind that formed all things from water. Thus, he placed the matter of things in moisture and established the principle and cause of birth in God. Pythagoras defined what God is: 'The mind that goes through all parts of the world and all nature, and is diffused, from which all living things take life'. Anaxagoras says that God is an infinite mind that moves by itself. Antisthenes says that there are many popular gods, but one natural God, that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes say that the highest God is the ether, to which opinion our poet assented. Chrysippus calls God the natural power endowed with divine reason, and sometimes divine necessity. Zenon also calls God the natural and divine law. Although the opinion of all these men is uncertain, it nevertheless looks to the same thing, that they agree there is one providence. For whether you say nature, or ether, or reason, or mind, or fatal necessity, or divine law, or anything else, it is the same as what we call God. Nor does the diversity of names hinder, since all things are referred to one thing by their signification. Aristotle, although he disagrees with himself and says and thinks contradictory things, nevertheless testifies that one mind presides over the world. Plato, who is judged to be the wisest of all, openly and plainly defends the monarchy, and does not name the ether, or reason, or nature, but calls him God, from whom this world was made perfect and wonderful. Cicero, following and imitating him in many things, frequently confesses God and calls him supreme in the books he wrote about the laws, arguing that the world is ruled by him, when he discusses the nature of the gods, in this way: 'Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore, it is necessary that the world is ruled by him. For God is not subject to any nature, nor is he obedient to it. Therefore, he himself rules all nature'. Because he is God, we do not doubt: nor can God himself, who is understood by us, be understood in any other way than as a certain mind, free and separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things. Seneca also, who was a most keen Stoic among the Romans, how often does he pursue the highest God with deserved praise! For when he was discussing premature death, he says: 'Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of the earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divine powers which we adore and worship are suspended?' Also in his Exhortations: 'When he laid the first foundations of this beautiful world and began to order it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although he himself had extended throughout his whole body, nevertheless, God generated the ministers of his kingdom'. And how many other things did he say about God, similar to ours! Which I now omit, because they are more opportune in other places. Now it is enough to demonstrate that men of the highest genius have touched upon the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were drawn back by the corrupt and perverse opinions of custom, by which they believed that there were other gods and that the things which God made for the use of men were to be held and worshiped as gods.
pass_b_english: We should set aside the prophets’ testimony, lest the proof appear inadequate to those who reject it entirely. Let us turn instead to the authors our opponents themselves invoke—the poets and philosophers—and call them as witnesses to the truth. From them we must establish one God, not because they possessed the truth, but because truth’s power is so great that no one can be so blind as to miss the divine clarity forced upon their eyes. The poets, though they decked the gods in verse and magnified their deeds with highest praise, still confess again and again that all things are held together and governed by a single spirit or mind. Orpheus, most ancient of the poets and a peer of the gods themselves—tradition says he sailed with the Argonauts alongside Castor and Hercules—calls the true and great God ‘Protogonos’, because nothing was generated before him, but all things were generated from him. He also names him ‘Phaneta’, because when nothing yet existed, he first appeared and stood forth from the infinite. Unable to conceive his origin and nature, Orpheus said he was born of vast air: ‘Protogonos Phaethon, son of immeasurable air’; he had nothing further to say. This God, he says, is the parent of all the gods, for whose sake he founded heaven and provided for his children a common dwelling and seat: ‘He built an imperishable house for the immortals’. Guided by nature and reason, Orpheus recognized a supreme power, the creator of heaven and earth. He could not name Jupiter as the first principle, since Jupiter was born of Saturn; nor Saturn, who was said to be born of heaven; nor dare he make heaven itself the first god, because he saw heaven as a world-element that itself required an author. This reasoning led him to that firstborn God, to whom he assigns and attributes sovereignty. Homer offers nothing for the truth, for he wrote of human, not divine, matters. Hesiod might have, since he compressed the gods’ genealogy into a single book; yet he gave no account that did not begin with Chaos—a confused mass of raw, disordered matter—when he ought first to have explained what Chaos is, and whence, when, and how it began to exist. For just as all things are ordered and fashioned by some craftsman, so this matter itself must have been fashioned by someone. Who made it, if not God, to whose power all things are subject? But Hesiod shrinks back, dreading the unknown truth. He did not pour out that song on Helicon by the Muses’ impulse, as he wished to seem, but came prepared and deliberate. Our first poet, Virgil, was not far from the truth. Of the highest God, whom he named Mind and Spirit, he wrote: ‘In the beginning the Spirit nourishes heaven and earth and the fields and the shining globe of the moon and the Titan stars; the Mind, infused throughout, stirs the whole mass and mingles with the great body’. And lest anyone mistake which Spirit wields such power, he declared elsewhere: ‘For God passes through all lands and sea-tracts and deep heaven; from him flocks and herds and men and every kind of wild beast, each living thing new-born, are summoned to life’. Ovid, too, at the start of his great work, without disguising the name, acknowledges that the world was ordered by God, whom he calls the world’s maker and craftsman of things. If Orpheus or our own poets, led by nature, had defended perpetually what they perceived, they would have held the same doctrine we follow, having grasped the truth. So much for the poets. Now to the philosophers, whose authority is weightier and judgment surer, because they are thought to have studied not fictions but the investigation of truth. Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages and said to be the first to seek natural causes, said water is the source from which all things are born, but God is the Mind that formed all things from water. Thus he placed the matter of things in moisture and fixed the principle and cause of generation in God. Pythagoras defined God as: ‘The Mind that pervades all parts of the world and all nature, diffused throughout, from which all living creatures receive life’. Anaxagoras says God is an infinite Mind that moves itself. Antisthenes grants many popular gods, but one natural God—that is, the craftsman of the whole. Cleanthes and Anaximenes name the highest God as Ether; our poet assented to this view: ‘Then the Almighty Father, with fertilizing rains, descended into the joyful lap of his Ether-bride, and the great offspring is nourished, mingled with the great body’. Chrysippus calls God the natural power endowed with divine reason, sometimes divine necessity; Zeno calls God the natural and divine law. Though all their opinions are uncertain, they converge on the same point: they agree that there is one Providence. Whether you call it Nature, or Ether, or Reason, or Mind, or Fatal Necessity, or Divine Law, or anything else, it is the same thing we call God. Nor does the diversity of names obstruct, since all are referred by their meaning to one reality. Aristotle, though he contradicts himself and says and thinks opposing things, still testifies that one Mind presides over the world. Plato, judged the wisest of all, defends the monarchy openly and plainly, and does not name Ether, or Reason, or Nature, but calls him God, from whom this world was made perfect and wonderful. Cicero, following and imitating him in many places, frequently confesses God and calls him Supreme in the books he wrote on the laws, arguing that the world is ruled by him when he discusses the nature of the gods: ‘Nothing is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be ruled by him. For God is subject to no nature, nor obedient to it. Therefore he himself rules all nature.’ That God exists we do not doubt; nor can God himself, as we understand him, be understood in any other way than as a certain Mind, free and separated from all mortal concretion, perceiving and moving all things. Seneca, the keenest Stoic among the Romans, how often does he extol the highest God with deserved praise! When discussing premature death he says: ‘Do you not understand the authority and majesty of your judge, the ruler of earth and heaven and all the gods, from whom those divine powers which we singly adore and worship are suspended?’ Also in his Exhortations: ‘When he laid the first foundations of this most beautiful world and began to order it, so that all things might go under their leaders, although he himself had extended through his whole body, nevertheless God generated the ministers of his kingdom.’ And how many other things he said about God, similar to ours! I omit them now, because they fit better elsewhere. For the present it is enough to show that men of the highest genius have touched the truth and almost grasped it, unless they were dragged back by custom’s corrupt and perverse opinions, by which they believed there were other gods and that the things God made for human use were to be held and worshipped as gods.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the complex philosophical arguments and the specific poetic quotations. All citations (Orpheus, Hesiod, Virgil/Maro, Ovid, Thales, Pythagoras, Anaxagoras, Antisthenes, Cleanthes, Anaximenes, Chrysippus, Zeno, Aristotle, Plato, Cicero, Seneca) are correctly handled. The distinction between 'protogonos' and 'Phaneta' is preserved. The translation of the Virgil/Maro passage and the Seneca passages matches the Latin source accurately.
